about: What if every undersea internet cable was cut? Long-form 16:9 stickman explainer, episode 1 of Tech, explained on YouTube. Narration first; every visual beat keys to its word times.

lines.text: You text a friend in London. "Landed yet?"
In under a second, it's there.
But to get there, your message dove to the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean.
It rode a beam of light, through a cable on the sea floor.
Now imagine every one of those cables snaps. All of them. At the same second.
What happens in the first minute? The first day? The first month?
What if every undersea internet cable was cut?
First, what's actually down there.
More than 600 cables, active and planned.
lines.say: More than six hundred cables, active and planned.

lines.text: Laid end to end, over 900,000 miles of them.
lines.say: Laid end to end, over nine hundred thousand miles of them.

lines.text: That's enough to wrap around the Earth about 37 times.
lines.say: That's enough to wrap around the Earth about thirty-seven times.

lines.text: And most of the way across the ocean, a cable is about as thick as a garden hose.
Inside it: a few strands of glass, each thinner than a hair, carrying pulses of light.
What about satellites?
For the United States, satellites are just 0.37 percent of all international capacity.
lines.say: For the United States, satellites are just zero point three seven percent of all international capacity.

lines.text: The rest goes through cables.
And cables break all the time. About 200 times a year.
lines.say: And cables break all the time. About two hundred times a year.

lines.text: Two thirds of those are accidents: fishing gear and ship anchors dragging across the sea floor.
Sharks? From 2007 to 2014, fish bites caused zero faults.
lines.say: Sharks? From two thousand seven to two thousand fourteen, fish bites caused zero faults.

lines.text: One cut is no big deal. The internet just routes around it.
But what if there's nothing left to route around?
Second one.
Your message to London never arrives.
Routers on the coast notice the dead links in a split second and look for another path.
There isn't one. Every road off the continent is gone.
Minute one. And here's the weird part: most of your phone still works.
Texts to people nearby still go through. Your local news still loads.
Big streaming services keep copies of popular shows on servers inside your country.
So your show keeps playing.
But tap a website that only lives overseas, and it spins. Forever.
Your video call to family abroad freezes, then drops.
Hour one. Now money starts to notice.
A tourist's card gets declined, because their bank is on another continent.
Traders in New York can't see prices in London.
Companies that keep their data in a cloud overseas go dark.
Satellites try to carry the load. But that's a river trying to squeeze through a straw.
And for some places, it's worse.
Islands with one or two cables are simply cut off from the world.
Day one. Sounds like science fiction? Parts of it already happened.
In 2008, cable cuts near Egypt knocked out about 70 percent of Egypt's link to the wider internet.
lines.say: In two thousand eight, cable cuts near Egypt knocked out about seventy percent of Egypt's link to the wider internet.

lines.text: India lost roughly half of its outbound connection.
In 2024, a sinking cargo ship in the Red Sea most likely dragged its anchor and cut three cables at once.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-four, a sinking cargo ship in the Red Sea most likely dragged its anchor and cut three cables at once.

lines.text: And in 2022, an undersea volcano in Tonga snapped the country's only international cable.
lines.say: And in twenty twenty-two, an undersea volcano in Tonga snapped the country's only international cable.

lines.text: The whole country fell back on a handful of satellite links.
Week one. So who fixes all this?
Only about 20 to 30 ships on Earth are dedicated cable repair ships.
lines.say: Only about twenty to thirty ships on Earth are dedicated cable repair ships.

lines.text: A ship sails to the break and drags a hook along the sea floor.
It lifts the cable up to the deck, and the crew splices the glass back together by hand.
Even for a single break, the typical repair takes about eight days just to start.
Now do the math. About 570 cables, about 25 ships.
lines.say: Now do the math. About five hundred seventy cables, about twenty-five ships.

lines.text: That's around 23 cables for every ship.
lines.say: That's around twenty-three cables for every ship.

lines.text: At even two weeks each, the last ones come back almost a year later.
Month one. Tonga's repair took five weeks.
The crew had to replace about 56 miles of cable.
lines.say: The crew had to replace about fifty-six miles of cable.

lines.text: Now picture that, at every cable, all at once.
So next time a message lands on the other side of the world, in a blink,
remember the trip it took: down to the ocean floor, through a glass thread inside a garden hose.
And somewhere out there, a ship is fixing one right now.
This is Tech, explained. Subscribe, and I'll show you how the rest of it works.
